content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to handle the parameter-efficient tuning problem by searching for custom designs (i.e., numbers of trainable parameters and the choices of parameter-efficient modules) for each downstream task. The proposed NOAH first trains a supernet for each task that includes visual prompts, Adapter modules, and LoRA modules of different lengths, then conduct an evolutionary search to get the optimal ones. The experimental results show that NOAH achieves the best performance on VTAB-1k benchmark and few-shot learning benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
* The motivation is intuitive. It is straightforward to apply custom design choices when adapting to different tasks, considering the different domain gaps and label space to pre-training data.
* I believe it is promising to explore the once-for-all (OFA) settings for task adaptation, which derives a set of models satisfying different parameter constraints. The paper is the first to explore this path and provides some important analysis and insights. 
* The paper is well-organized and has a clear presentation.

Weakness:
* Although the motivation is good, the proposed approach has limited novelty. The idea of combining several parameter-efficient modules to seek higher performance is overly simple and lacks insight. The authors argue that the parameter-efficient modules are complementary, which contradicts the findings in [A] that these modules share very similar forms, and also contradicts [B] which claims that the downstream task can be described by a low intrinsic dimension (that can be captured by any of the prompt modules, i.e., prompt tuning, Adapter, and LoRA). A discussion with [A] and [B] would be appreciated.

* Although the paper follows the once-for-all settings, it only provides a single result for each of the benchmarks. As mentioned in strength, the key ability for the OFA settings is to provide a set of models under various parameter constraints. I believe to fully demonstrate the superiority of NOAH; it’s necessary to show results under different parameter constraints.

[A] He, Junxian, et al. "Towards a unified view of parameter-efficient transfer learning." ICLR (2022).
[B]  Aghajanyan, Armen, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Sonal Gupta. "Intrinsic dimensionality explains the effectiveness of language model fine-tuning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2012.13255 (2020).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The motivation is intuitive. Although the motivation is good, the proposed approach has limited novelty. Please see my detailed comments.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies using neural architecture search (NAS) for parameter efficient tuning method in the computer vision domain. Specifically, the authors consider a search space consisting of parameterized components from hand-designed SoTA parameter efficient tuning methods. The authors use a supernet approach (NOAH) to encode this search space and use evolutionary strategy to search the high accuracy subnets from the supernet.

The authors compare to grid search of structural hyperparameters (e.g. dimensions) of individual tuning methods. They show that the NAS approach over all the tuning methods shows superior accuracy on fine-tuning, few-shot and domain generalization tasks across vision benchmarks, at similar GPU compute hours.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The empirical accuracy achieved by the NAS on domain generalization is very noticeable. A ~5-~10% improvement for the domain generalization should be considered substantial. My only question on this point is that if the comparison to VPT, Adaptor and LoRA is at a fair basis with similar trainable parameters or overall GPU hours to produce the model (Including the entire search time and training time when applicable). It would be great if the authors could clarify on this.

2. I think the empirical discoveries on searched architectures are intrinsically interesting and should potentially be invested more. E.g. the authors discovered that shallow layers prefer to be untrained because the searched architecture does not have the "prompt modules" in the shallow layers.

Weakness:

1. On the VTAB-1k experiment, the author compares the NAS model to Adapter and LoRa baselines which has 2-3x less trainable parameters than the NAS approach. If the claim is oriented towards accuracy comparison at same amount of trainable parameters, it needs to compare at closer trainable parameter counts across the methods. If the claim is oriented towards accuracy comparison at the same GPU hours to produce the models, the experiment should consider the LoRA* and Adaptor* numbers which include grid search on structural hyperparameters.

2. I think the methodological novelty and impact is limited by the fact that it only consider the search space of 3 well-known parameter efficient method. Specifically, the results shows the benefits of combining existing techniques and auto search their parameterization. The impact would be limited compared to do a NAS on a systematically designed search space which is beyond what the community already knows. Such an approach could trigger the discovery of previously unknown design pattern and design decisions for practitioners.

3. Minor thoughts: I would highly suggest the authors to include the full fine tuning numbers for major experiments to give a full picture of the efficiency accuracy trade-off. Understand that some of the parameter efficient method actually generalize better, but a full exposure of these numbers would give the readers a full picture to evaluate and make decisions when they choose between different type of methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think the writing is overall clear but need some more precision on claims

1. When claiming accuracy advantages, I think clarify the comparison basis / constraints is very important. E.g. is it w.r.t. similar trained parameter count, similar GPU hours to generate the model.

2. Minor question: In the NOAH approach, does it still require training in the Search phase in table 3? Or is it purely evaluating on different subnets in the search phase?
content.summary_of_the_review:
I recommended marginally-below-acceptance due to the considerations on the following factors:

1) the necessary improvements on the experiment design and 
2) the limited technical novelty and discovery impact due to focusing on a search space only covering known techniques. Please refer to the strength and weakness section for detailed justification.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper combines 3 existing VL adaptation methods, that serve as search space over which a search is performed using Autoformer. A series of evaluations and ablations analyze the behavior of this components across the network. When evaluated the described method improves the state-of-the-art results in 10/19 datasets. However, the novelty is overall incremental and some comparisons are missing.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- Good overall structure that is easy to read.
- The concept in itself, of finding the optimal configuration for adapting VL models is interesting.
- Interesting ablation studies (such as the distribution of each method across different layers).

Weaknesses:

1. Incremental novelty: while the  idea of automatically finding the best way of adapting large scale models is sound, the novelty of the proposed approach is small. The method simply combines a previously proposed NAS technique (Autoformer) with 3 VL adaptation methods, without making any notable changes.

2. Inconcludent results:

 - Typically, NAS methods are compared against two baselines: random search (multiple runs) and hand crafted. The hand crafted one are constructed by careful engineering on a per-dataset basis by a practitioner. Without extensive evidence of outperforming such baselines its hard to judge the quality of the solutions found.

- Unclear what is the reason for underperforming on nearly 50% of the datasets (9/19). This  suggests that the current approach may not be reliable/consistent enough to be used in practice compared with a vanilla method.

3. Others:

- What is the zero-shot performance of such networks? Is this property of the VL models preserved?

- Can this work be applied on other architectures beyond ViT, or is it ViT-specific?

- What is the impact of using just one, or two of this methods during the search, instead of all 3?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written, however the novelty is incremental and some evaluations, against certain noteworthy baselines are missing.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is well written, however as its a vanilla implementation of 3 adaptation methods and one  NAS approach its novelty is incremental. Moreover some important evaluations are missing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims at parameter-efficient learning in vision transformers, which is addressed by neural architecture search. Specifically, the authors integrate the embedding dimensions and the depths of VPT, Adapter, and LoRA into the search space, which is then solved by a one-shot evolutionary search algorithm with weight entanglement. The experiments have been performed on various datasets, demonstrating the promising performance for transfer learning, few-shot learning, and domain generalization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Promising performance with extensive experiments.
2. This paper is well written and easy to understand.

Weaknesses:
My main concern for this paper is about the novelty. This paper simply combines AutoFormer, Adapter, LoRA, and VPT with all the intact existing components. Specifically, this paper directly reuses the exact search algorithm of AutoFormer, including the evolutionary search and the weight entanglement in the supernet. Additionally, the search space, i.e., the individual design of the embedding dimensions and the depths of VPT, Adapter, and LoRA, has also been studied in the ablation of the corresponding paper, respectively. Moreover, the architecture of VPT, Adapter, and LoRA also remains the same. Therefore, this paper seems more like an experimental paper combining intact existing components, but without sufficient novelty or insight of the algorithm.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This paper is well-written and easy to understand.

Quality, Novelty, Originality: I would consider those as the main concern of the paper, as the paper simply integrates several existing components to perform an existing search algorithm on a combination of existing search spaces. Please refer to the details of the Strength And Weaknesses section.

Reproducibility: This paper would have good reproducibility as most components of the proposed method are existed and intact.
content.summary_of_the_review: On one hand, this paper is well written and extensive experiments have been carried out; but on the other hand, all the components of the algorithm have been proposed before and this paper reuse those intact, which makes this paper more like an experimental paper and lack of novelty and insight of the algorithm.
